ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Ketone bodies are water‑soluble fuel molecules produced by the liver during carbohydrate shortage. Excess accumulation causes high‑anion‑gap metabolic acidosis, especially in uncontrolled diabetes or prolonged fasting.

sections.p: The liver converts fatty‑acid‑derived acetyl‑CoA into three ketone bodies that can cross the blood‑brain barrier and supply energy when glucose is scarce.
b: Acetoacetate (AA) and β‑hydroxybutyrate (β‑HB) are true acids; acetone is volatile and exhaled.
Ketone production rises when insulin is low and glucagon is high.

sections.p: During fasting or insulin deficiency, lipolysis releases fatty acids; hepatic β‑oxidation yields acetyl‑CoA, which exceeds TCA capacity and is diverted to ketogenesis.
b: Acetyl‑CoA → HMG‑CoA → acetoacetate → β‑HB (reduced) or acetone (spontaneous decarboxylation).
β‑HB is the predominant circulating ketone (≈80%).

sections.p: Insulin suppresses, while glucagon, catecholamines, and cortisol stimulate hepatic HMG‑CoA synthase, the rate‑limiting enzyme of ketogenesis.
b: High NAD⁺/NADH ratio favors β‑HB formation.

sections.p: When production outpaces peripheral utilization, ketone bodies accumulate, causing high‑anion‑gap metabolic acidosis (ketoacidosis).
b: Uncontrolled type 1 diabetes (most common cause worldwide).
Prolonged fasting, starvation, or very low‑carb diets.
Rare: inborn errors of metabolism (e.g., HMG‑CoA lyase deficiency).

sections.p: Ketoacidosis presents with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, and altered mental status; it can be rapidly fatal if untreated.
b: High anion‑gap metabolic acidosis: AG > 12 mmol/L, β‑HB > 3 mmol/L.
Serum glucose > 250 mg/dL in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
Serum β‑HB is more sensitive than urine ketones.

t.b: Quantifies ketone burden; >3 mmol/L confirms significant ketoacidosis.
Detects metabolic acidosis; pH < 7.3 and bicarbonate < 15 mmol/L indicate severe DKA.
Identifies high‑anion‑gap; guides fluid and electrolyte replacement.

sections.p: Focus on pathophysiology, diagnostic thresholds, and emergency management steps.
b: DKA diagnostic triad: hyperglycemia, ketonemia, metabolic acidosis.
Alcoholic ketoacidosis: low/normal glucose, high β‑HB, history of binge drinking.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain, vomiting, or altered consciousness with known diabetes or recent binge drinking.
Rapid breathing (Kussmaul) and fruity breath indicating possible ketoacidosis.

faq.q: Why is β‑hydroxybutyrate measured instead of acetoacetate?
faq.a: β‑HB is the predominant circulating ketone and rises earlier; it reflects true ketone load better than urine dipsticks.

faq.q: Can ketone bodies be used as a therapeutic fuel?
faq.a: Yes, in controlled ketogenic diets for epilepsy; however, uncontrolled production is harmful.

faq.q: Why does ketoacidosis cause a high anion gap?
faq.a: Unmeasured anions (β‑HB, acetoacetate) increase the gap while chloride remains unchanged.
